content.title: About
content.content: The T‑bone steak is a large cut of beef that includes a portion of the tenderloin and a portion of the strip loin, separated by a T‑shaped bone. This version uses only the lean part of the meat, with visible fat trimmed away. The steak offers a rich beef flavor, firm texture, and the characteristic bone that helps retain juiciness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The T‑bone is considered one of the most “royal” steaks because it combines two different muscles in one cut.
A lean T‑bone contains less fat than the traditional version but still retains much of the beefy taste.
The T‑shaped bone helps keep the meat moist during high‑heat cooking.
T‑bone steaks are a staple on many upscale restaurant menus, often grilled or pan‑seared.
In the United States the T‑bone ranks among the top‑5 most popular steak cuts.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Lean T‑bone provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals contribute to immune function and antioxidant defense.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The lean cut is suitable for low‑fat diets while still providing essential nutrients.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Even lean beef contains cholesterol, so people with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor harmful bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella). Cook to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C (145 °F).

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Beef is high in purines, which can exacerbate gout in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The T‑bone is best cooked over high heat: grill, cast‑iron grill pan, or broiler. Let the steak come to room temperature, season with salt and pepper, then sear 3‑4 minutes per side for medium‑rare. Rest the meat 5‑10 minutes before slicing to allow juices to redistribute. Serve with grilled vegetables, a light herb sauce, or a simple vinaigrette.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the T‑bone steak refrigerated at 0‑4 °C in its original packaging or an airtight container for 3‑5 days. For longer storage, freeze in a vacuum‑sealed bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw frozen steak in the refrigerator, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Potatoes (Solanum tuberosum) are starchy underground tubers of a plant native to the Andes of South America. They have been cultivated for thousands of years and are now one of the world's most important food crops. Potatoes have thin skin and mild-tasting white to yellow flesh, and they are boiled, baked, mashed, fried, and used in countless dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes were domesticated in the Andes region thousands of years ago and reached Europe in the 16th century.
Thousands of potato varieties exist, with skins and flesh in white, yellow, red, and purple.
Potatoes belong to the nightshade family, as do tomatoes, peppers, and eggplants.
A potato is a tuber, which is a swollen underground stem that stores starch.
Waxy potatoes hold their shape when cooked, while starchy potatoes become fluffy.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide more potassium than many other vegetables, which supports normal blood pressure.

items.title: Provides vitamin C
items.content: Potatoes contain vitamin C, which supports the immune system and skin.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 supports normal metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Provides fiber and resistant starch
items.content: Eating the skin adds fiber, and cooked and cooled potatoes contain resistant starch, which supports digestion.

items.title: Filling source of energy
items.content: Potatoes are rich in carbohydrates and can be a filling part of meals.

items.title: Green or sprouted potatoes
items.content: Green skin and sprouts contain solanine, a natural toxin. Cut away green parts and sprouts, and discard heavily green or bitter potatoes.

items.title: Acrylamide
items.content: Frying, roasting, or baking at very high temperatures can form acrylamide, so avoid over-browning.

items.title: High glycemic effect
items.content: Potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, so portion size and preparation matter for people monitoring blood sugar.

items.title: Fat and salt in fried products
items.content: French fries, chips, and processed potato products often contain a lot of fat and sodium.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Potatoes can be boiled, steamed, baked, roasted, mashed, or added to soups, stews, salads, and casseroles. Eating them with the skin on adds fiber. Baking, boiling, or steaming is generally a lighter choice than deep frying.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store potatoes in a cool, dark, well-ventilated place, away from onions and sunlight, because light causes greening and the refrigerator can turn their starch to sugar. Keep them unwashed until use. Check regularly and discard any that are soft, moldy, or heavily sprouted.

content.title: About
content.content: Strawberry milk with reduced fat (2 %) is a beverage made from whole cow’s milk to which natural strawberry flavor and a small amount of sugar are added. The low‑fat version retains most of the protein and calcium typical of milk while containing minimal fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Strawberry flavor is often derived from a concentrated berry extract rather than artificial aromatics.
Low‑fat milk is easier to digest, making it popular among athletes and weight‑conscious consumers.
Strawberries are rich in vitamin C, some of which remains after the mild heat treatment used in production.
In the United States such drinks are frequently classified as “milk beverages” rather than plain milk because of added flavorings.
Reduced‑fat milk has a longer shelf life than whole milk due to lower fat content, which is less prone to oxidation.

items.title: High in calcium
items.content: Strawberry milk retains a high calcium level, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: With only 2 % fat, the beverage helps control calorie intake, useful for diet‑focused eating.

items.title: Source of vitamin D
items.content: Fortified vitamin D aids calcium absorption and supports immune function.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Milk protein supports muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Strawberry extract adds a modest amount of vitamin C, an antioxidant.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Like any milk, it contains lactose, which can cause discomfort for those with lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein or whey proteins.

items.title: Added sugar
items.content: A small amount of sugar is added for taste; people monitoring blood glucose should consider this.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Strawberry extract can slightly increase the drink’s acidity, potentially affecting tooth enamel.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Strawberry milk can be enjoyed on its own, used in smoothies, poured over oatmeal or cereal, and incorporated into baking recipes as a flavored liquid substitute.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Do not freeze, as this may alter texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Thousand Island Dressing, Light is a reduced‑fat version of the classic Thousand Island sauce. It is made with low‑fat mayonnaise, tomato paste, vinegar, sweet paprika and aromatic spices, but with fewer fats and calories. It has the characteristic sweet‑tangy flavor and is suitable for diet‑friendly meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original Thousand Island dressing originated in the United States in the early 20th century and is named after the Thousand Islands region.
The light version was developed in the 1990s in response to growing demand for lower‑calorie products.
Light recipes often incorporate yogurt or low‑fat kefir to reduce fat content.
The sauce retains its flavor profile in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks.
Thousand Island Dressing, Light is frequently used in diet menus at fast‑food chains.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: Thanks to reduced fat and the use of low‑fat dairy, the dressing contains far fewer calories than the traditional version.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Tomato paste and vinegar provide vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: If yogurt or kefir is used, the dressing can contribute to a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Reduced sodium
items.content: The light formulation typically contains less salt, beneficial for blood pressure control.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes and spices supply lycopene and other antioxidants that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: When yogurt or kefir is part of the recipe, people with milk allergy should be cautious.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: A small amount of sugar may be added for sweetness, which should be considered by individuals with diabetes.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Vinegar makes the dressing acidic; those with acid reflux should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Shelf life after opening
items.content: Once opened, the dressing loses freshness quickly; keep it refrigerated and use within 7‑10 days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thousand Island Dressing, Light is perfect for salads, vegetable sticks, sandwiches, sushi rolls, and seafood. It can be used as a marinade for chicken or turkey, or added to burgers as a lighter alternative to regular mayo.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dressing in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C in a tightly sealed container. Once opened, use within 7‑10 days. Do not freeze, as the texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: A whole grain waffle is a fast‑food style product made from whole‑grain flour, eggs, milk and a modest amount of sugar. It features a crisp exterior and a light, airy interior, offering a pleasant taste while delivering higher fiber and nutrient content than regular waffles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain waffles are often offered in fast‑food restaurants as a healthier alternative to standard waffles.
The batter is cooked in a waffle iron, where hot plates create the characteristic grid pattern.
Waffles can be enriched with seeds, nuts, or berries to boost flavor and nutrition.
Waffles originated in medieval Europe but became mass‑produced in the United States in the early 20th century.
They are served with fruit, yogurt, honey, or even as a sandwich with savory fillings.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour retains bran and germ, increasing dietary fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide a steadier blood‑sugar response compared with simple sugars.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Waffles contain thiamine, niacin and folate, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Whole grain waffles supply magnesium, iron and zinc, supporting muscle function and immunity.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: When prepared in a waffle iron without excessive oil, trans‑fat content remains minimal.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Made from wheat, the waffle contains gluten and is unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some recipes add notable sugar; portion control is advisable, especially for diabetics.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Although less calorie‑dense than regular waffles, it still provides significant energy and can contribute to weight gain if over‑consumed.

items.title: Heat‑induced compounds
items.content: Over‑cooking may produce acrylamide, a potentially harmful compound.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the waffle warm with berries, fruit puree, yogurt, nut butter or honey. It can also be used as a base for savory sandwiches with lean cheese, turkey, or vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked waffles in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in a toaster or microwave before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Wasabi paste is a spicy condiment made from the root of the wasabi plant (Wasabia japonica) or from a blend of horseradish, mustard, and food coloring. The paste is bright green, aromatic, and delivers a sharp, slightly sweet heat that hits the nose as well as the palate.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: True wasabi is cultivated in Japan, mainly in the cool, humid mountain streams of Honshu.
Only about 5 % of commercially available wasabi products are 100 % genuine; most are horseradish‑based imitations.
Traditionally it is served with sushi and sashimi to enhance the flavor of raw fish and cleanse the palate.
The root contains isothiocyanates, which give wasabi its characteristic heat and aroma.
Wasabi has natural antibacterial properties, making it a useful accompaniment in sushi bars.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Isothiocyanates in wasabi help neutralize free radicals, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: Compounds in the paste stimulate immune‑cell activity and may boost the body’s defense mechanisms.

items.title: Antibacterial action
items.content: Wasabi inhibits the growth of certain pathogenic bacteria, which is beneficial when eating raw fish.

items.title: Digestive stimulation
items.content: The sharp flavor promotes gastric juice secretion, aiding digestion.

items.title: Cardiovascular health
items.content: Studies suggest isothiocyanates can improve lipid profiles and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to wasabi or its substitutes.

items.title: Mucosal irritation
items.content: Large amounts of the hot paste can cause burning sensations in the mouth, stomach, or intestines.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ready‑made commercial pastes often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Fake product
items.content: Horseradish‑based imitations may include artificial colors and preservatives that lack the health benefits of true wasabi.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Wasabi paste is typically served in small dollops alongside sushi, sashimi, rolls, or grilled dishes. It can be stirred into sauces, marinades, soups, and salads for extra heat. When using a horseradish imitation, a splash of lemon juice adds a brighter flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the paste in a sealed jar in the refrigerator. Properly stored, it retains its flavor for up to 6 months. Discard if the aroma becomes overly sharp or the color fades.
